en: Itivuttaka 97: Tikanipāta, Pañcamavagga (The Fifth Chapter) Thus it was said by the Blessed One; having thus spoken, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and went to his dwelling. Thereupon, the venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would explain to me in brief the meaning of this statement that was uttered by the Blessed One: ‘Monks, I shall teach you the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; I shall reveal the holy life that is perfectly complete and pure. “Ānanda, what do you think? Is form permanent or impermanent? “Impermanent, venerable sir. “But is that which is impermanent suffering or happiness? “Suffering, venerable sir. “But is it fitting to regard that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change as: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’? “No, venerable sir. [The same is repeated for feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness. “Therefore, Ānanda, whatever is form—whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all form should be seen with right wisdom exactly as it is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. Whatever is feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness—whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all consciousness should be seen with right wisdom exactly as it is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. Seeing this thus as it really is with right wisdom, Ānanda, a noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with volitional formations, and disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. Through liberation, there is the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being. “This, Ānanda, is the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; it reveals the holy life that is perfectly complete and pure. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, the venerable Ānanda delighted in the Blessed One’s words. Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks! “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this: “Monks, I shall teach you the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; I shall reveal the holy life that is perfectly complete and pure. Listen and attend closely; I shall speak. “Yes, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Monks, what is the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which reveals the holy life that is perfectly complete and pure? It is this: the discourse on the threefold training. And what, monks, is the training in higher virtue? Here, a monk is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults; having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. This is called the training in higher virtue. And what, monks, is the training in higher mind? Here, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. With the subsiding of thought and examination, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and has rapture and happiness born of concentration. With the fading away of rapture, he dwells equanimous and, mindful and clearly comprehending, experiences happiness with the body; he enters and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the Noble Ones declare: ‘He is equanimous, mindful, and dwells happily. With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.

This is called the training in higher mind. And what, monks, is the training in higher wisdom? Here, a monk understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This is called the training in higher wisdom. When, monks, a noble disciple is thus endowed with these three trainings, he is called a noble disciple who is accomplished in virtue, accomplished in concentration, and accomplished in wisdom; one who has reached the ultimate end of the holy life, one who has completed the task, laid down the burden, attained his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and become liberated through final knowledge. This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and went to his dwelling. The Discourse on Beautiful Virtue.
This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant, so I have heard:

“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is beautiful in virtue, beautiful in Dhamma, and beautiful in wisdom is called, in this Dhamma and discipline, ‘one who is complete, one who has lived the holy life, the supreme person.’”
And how, monks, is a monk of beautiful virtue?

Here, monks, a monk is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains himself in the rules of training.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk is of beautiful virtue.
Thus he is one of virtuous conduct. And how is he one of beautiful nature?
Here, monks, a monk dwells devoted to the practice of developing the seven factors of enlightenment.
In this way, monks, a monk is one of beautiful character and beautiful nature.
Thus he is of beautiful virtue and beautiful nature.
And how is he one of beautiful wisdom?

“Here, bhikkhus, with the destruction of the taints, a bhikkhu dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it.
In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one of beautiful wisdom.

Thus, one who is of beautiful virtue, of beautiful Dhamma, and of beautiful wisdom is called, in this Dhamma and Discipline, ‘one who is complete, one who has lived the holy life, the supreme person.’”
The Blessed One spoke this matter.
Regarding this, it is said:
“By whom, through body or speech,..."
There is no misdeed committed by the mind;
indeed, they call such a modest monk one of virtuous character.
He whose states are well-developed,
leading to the seven forms of enlightenment—
him indeed they call one of beautiful character.
They call him a monk free from restlessness,
who understands here and now the destruction of his own suffering.
Him indeed they call a monk of noble wisdom, free from taints,
endowed with those qualities.
"Free from distress, with doubts severed,
unattached, and having abandoned everything— of him they say he is the one for the whole world."
This matter was also spoken by the Blessed One; thus have I heard.
The eighth.
